tracks.project_name: FitPulse: Modern Mobile Fitness & Workout Companion
tracks.tagline: Build a simple workout tracker app where you can plan workouts, log them, and see your weekly progress.

1.title: Home Screen & Workout List with Widgets
1.goal: Set up Flutter and build the first two static screens of FitPulse: a home dashboard and a list of workouts. Everything uses hardcoded data this week, so you can focus completely on how widgets and layouts fit together.
learn: How a Flutter app is structured: `main()`, `MaterialApp`, `Scaffold` and the widget tree
Layout widgets: `Column`, `Row`, `Padding`, `Container`, `Expanded` and `SizedBox`
Showing lists of data with `ListView.builder` and `Card`/`ListTile`
Creating a simple Dart model class and your own reusable widget
steps: Install Flutter, run `flutter doctor`, then create the project with `flutter create fitpulse` and run the counter app once to confirm your setup works.
Pick where you will run the app: an Android emulator, your own phone over USB, or Chrome with `flutter run -d chrome` if your laptop is low on RAM.
Delete the counter code and build a `HomeScreen` with an `AppBar`, a greeting, and a row of three summary cards (for example: workouts this week, minutes, streak) using hardcoded numbers.
Create a `Workout` class with `name`, `category`, `durationMinutes` and `isDone`, and make a hardcoded list of 5-6 workouts.
Build a `WorkoutListScreen` that shows the list with `ListView.builder`, using an icon and colour per category.
Pull the repeated card UI into its own `WorkoutCard` widget in a separate file so the list code stays short.
Add a `BottomNavigationBar` to switch between Home and Workouts, then set a colour theme in `ThemeData` so both screens look consistent.
Push the project to a GitHub repo with a README that includes a screenshot.
deliverables: A Flutter project in a public GitHub repo
A Home screen with summary cards and a Workouts screen with a scrollable list
A reusable `WorkoutCard` widget and a `Workout` model class
A README with setup steps and at least one screenshot
done_when: The app runs without errors on an emulator, phone or Chrome
The bottom navigation switches between the Home and Workouts screens
The workout list is built from a Dart list with `ListView.builder`, not copy-pasted widgets
The workout card UI lives in its own widget file
The repo contains a README with a screenshot
hints: Use hot reload (press `r` in the terminal) constantly; it is the fastest way to learn layouts by trial and error.
If you see a yellow-black overflow stripe, wrap the content in `Expanded` or make the screen scrollable with `SingleChildScrollView`.
You can practise individual widgets in the browser at [DartPad](https://dartpad.dev) before adding them to your app.
The widget catalog in the [Flutter docs](https://docs.flutter.dev) shows every layout widget with a picture.
1.stretch: Add a simple circular progress indicator on the home screen showing 'workouts done this week out of your weekly goal'.
post_highlights: Built the first screens of a Flutter fitness app with a dashboard and workout list
Created a reusable workout card widget and a Dart model class
Set up bottom navigation and a consistent app theme using Material widgets

2.title: Add Workouts with Forms & Navigation
2.goal: Make FitPulse interactive: users can add new workouts through a form, open a workout's detail screen, and mark it as done. This week teaches you how Flutter apps change what is on screen when data changes.
learn: The difference between `StatelessWidget` and `StatefulWidget`, and when to call `setState`
Moving between screens with `Navigator.push` and `Navigator.pop`, including passing data back
Building forms with `Form`, `TextFormField`, `DropdownButtonFormField` and validators
Updating a list in memory and seeing the UI refresh
steps: Convert the screen that owns the workout list into a `StatefulWidget` so the list can change.
Add a checkbox or tap action on each workout that toggles `isDone` inside `setState`, and confirm the Home summary numbers update too.
Create a `WorkoutDetailScreen` that receives a `Workout` through its constructor and shows all its details; open it with `Navigator.push` when a card is tapped.
Add a `FloatingActionButton` that opens an `AddWorkoutScreen` with a form for name, category (dropdown) and duration.
Add validators: name must not be empty and duration must be a positive number; show error messages under the fields.
On save, return the new `Workout` with `Navigator.pop(context, workout)` and add it to the list in the previous screen.
Add a delete option (for example swipe-to-delete with `Dismissible`) and show a `SnackBar` confirming the action.
Record a short screen recording of adding, completing and deleting a workout.
deliverables: An Add Workout form with validation
A Workout Detail screen opened from the list
Mark-as-done and delete actions that update the UI immediately
A 30-60 second screen recording of the flow
done_when: Submitting the form with an empty name or invalid duration shows an error and does not save
A valid new workout appears in the list right after saving
Tapping a workout opens its detail screen and the back button returns to the list
Marking a workout as done updates the summary card on the Home screen
Deleting a workout removes it and shows a SnackBar
hints: If the UI does not update, check that you changed the data inside `setState(() { ... })` and not outside it.
Use a `TextEditingController` or the form's `onSaved` callback to read field values, and dispose controllers in `dispose()`.
To share the list between Home and Workouts for now, keep it in the parent widget that holds the bottom navigation and pass it down.
Search 'Flutter cookbook forms' and 'Flutter cookbook navigation' in the [Flutter docs](https://docs.flutter.dev) for short worked examples.
2.stretch: Add a filter row of `ChoiceChip`s at the top of the list to show only one category at a time.
post_highlights: Added a validated form to create new workouts in my Flutter app
Implemented screen navigation with data passed between screens
Used StatefulWidget and setState to mark workouts done and delete them with instant UI updates

3.title: Save Data Locally & Workout History
3.goal: Right now all workouts disappear when the app restarts. This week you save them on the device and add a history of completed workouts, handling loading and errors properly so the app never shows a blank or broken screen.
learn: Local storage on the device with `shared_preferences` or Hive
Converting objects to and from JSON with `toJson()` and `fromJson()`
Async code in Dart: `Future`, `async` and `await`
Showing loading, empty and error states in the UI
steps: Choose one storage option: `shared_preferences` (simplest, stores a JSON string) or Hive (a small local database); both work on Android and Chrome.
Add `toJson()` and a `fromJson()` factory to your `Workout` class and test them with a quick `print` before connecting storage.
Write a small `WorkoutStorage` class with `loadWorkouts()` and `saveWorkouts()` methods so the rest of the app does not care how data is stored.
Load workouts when the app starts and show a `CircularProgressIndicator` until loading finishes.
Call `saveWorkouts()` after every add, toggle and delete, then restart the app completely to confirm the data is still there.
Add a `completedAt` date to workouts and build a History screen listing completed workouts grouped or sorted by date.
Wrap loading in `try/catch`: if saved data is corrupted, show a friendly message and start with an empty list instead of crashing, and show an empty-state message when there are no workouts.
deliverables: Workouts that persist across full app restarts
A `WorkoutStorage` class that handles saving and loading
A History screen showing completed workouts with dates
Loading, empty and error states in the UI
done_when: Adding a workout, fully closing the app and reopening it still shows that workout
Completed workouts appear on the History screen with the date they were completed
A loading indicator is visible while data loads
With no workouts saved, the list shows a helpful empty-state message instead of a blank screen
Storage errors are caught and do not crash the app
hints: Hot reload keeps in-memory data, so always test persistence with a full stop and restart of the app.
`sqflite` does not work on Chrome; if you run on the web, stick with `shared_preferences` or Hive.
Store dates as ISO strings with `toIso8601String()` and read them back with `DateTime.parse()`.
Find packages and their example code on [pub.dev](https://pub.dev).
3.stretch: Add a simple rest timer screen that counts down from a chosen number of seconds using `Timer.periodic`.
post_highlights: Added local data persistence to my Flutter fitness app so workouts survive restarts
Built a workout history screen using JSON serialisation and async Dart code
Handled loading, empty and error states for a smoother user experience

4.title: Provider, Weekly Chart & Release Build
4.goal: Finish FitPulse as a portfolio-ready app. You will move your data into a simple Provider so any screen can use it, add a weekly progress chart, polish the design, and produce an installable build with a demo video.
learn: Simple app-wide state management with `provider` and `ChangeNotifier`
Drawing a bar chart from your own data with a chart package such as `fl_chart`
Adding a dark theme and small polish details
Building a release APK or a web build
steps: Create a `WorkoutProvider extends ChangeNotifier` that holds the list, calls your `WorkoutStorage`, and calls `notifyListeners()` after every change.
Wrap your app in `ChangeNotifierProvider` and replace the list you were passing down through constructors with `context.watch` and `context.read`.
Check every feature from weeks 1-3 still works before adding anything new.
Add a Progress screen with a bar chart showing total workout minutes for each of the last 7 days, calculated from your saved data.
Add a dark theme with `darkTheme` and a toggle switch, plus an app name and icon so it looks finished.
Build a release with `flutter build apk --release` (or `flutter build web` if you do not have the Android SDK) and test the build.
Update the README with features, screenshots, how to run it, and what you learned, then record a 60-second demo.
deliverables: App state managed with Provider
A Progress screen with a 7-day bar chart
A release APK (attached to a GitHub Release) or a web build
A polished README and a 60-second demo video
done_when: Workout data is read and changed through a Provider, not passed through constructors
The chart shows correct minutes for the last 7 days and updates when a workout is completed
Light and dark themes both look readable
A release APK or web build is available from the repo
The README explains features, setup and includes screenshots
hints: Use `context.watch<WorkoutProvider>()` inside `build` to listen for changes, and `context.read` inside button callbacks.
For the chart, first compute a simple `List<double>` of 7 values and print it, then feed it to the chart widget.
You can attach the APK file to a GitHub Release so recruiters can download it; see [GitHub Docs](https://docs.github.com).
The deployment section of the [Flutter docs](https://docs.flutter.dev) explains Android and web builds.
4.stretch: Add a daily reminder with a local notifications package, or write two widget tests for the Add Workout form.
post_highlights: Completed FitPulse, a Flutter workout tracker with local storage and Provider state management
Built a weekly progress bar chart and a dark theme
Shipped a release build with a documented README and demo video

tracks.project_name: WalletWave: Personal Finance & Smart Budget Tracker
tracks.tagline: Build an expense tracker app that records your income and spending and shows where your money goes each month.

1.title: Balance Dashboard & Transaction List
1.goal: Set up Flutter and build the main screen of WalletWave: a balance card at the top and a list of recent transactions below it. You will use hardcoded sample data so you can focus on widgets and layout.
learn: How a Flutter app is structured: `main()`, `MaterialApp`, `Scaffold` and the widget tree
Layout widgets: `Column`, `Row`, `Container`, `Padding` and `Expanded`
Displaying lists with `ListView.builder` and `ListTile`
Creating a Dart model class and formatting numbers as currency
steps: Install Flutter, run `flutter doctor`, create the project with `flutter create walletwave`, and run the default app once to confirm everything works.
Choose where to run the app: Android emulator, a real phone over USB, or Chrome with `flutter run -d chrome` if your laptop is low on RAM.
Create a `Transaction` class with `title`, `amount`, `category`, `date` and `isExpense`, and make a hardcoded list of about 8 transactions.
Build a `DashboardScreen` with a balance card showing total balance, total income and total expenses, calculated from the list rather than typed in.
Below the card, show the transactions with `ListView.builder`, using a category icon, the date, and red or green amounts for expenses and income.
Move the transaction row into its own `TransactionTile` widget file and format amounts in rupees (for example with the `intl` package).
Push to a public GitHub repo with a README and a screenshot.
deliverables: A Flutter project in a public GitHub repo
A dashboard with a balance card and a transaction list
A `Transaction` model and a reusable `TransactionTile` widget
A README with setup steps and a screenshot
done_when: The app runs without errors on an emulator, phone or Chrome
Balance, income and expense totals are calculated from the transaction list
Expenses and income are visually different (colour or sign)
The list uses `ListView.builder` and the row UI is its own widget
The README includes a screenshot
hints: Use hot reload (`r` in the terminal) to try layout changes quickly.
Use `fold` or a simple `for` loop to add up amounts; print the result first to check your maths.
Try widgets in the browser at [DartPad](https://dartpad.dev) if running the full app is slow on your laptop.
The widget catalog in the [Flutter docs](https://docs.flutter.dev) is the quickest way to find the right widget.
1.stretch: Add a horizontal row of category chips above the list showing how many transactions each category has.
post_highlights: Built the dashboard of a Flutter expense tracker with a live balance card
Displayed transactions with a reusable list tile widget and rupee formatting
Calculated income, expense and balance totals from a Dart data model

2.title: Add, Edit & Delete Transactions
2.goal: Make WalletWave interactive so users can add, edit and delete transactions through a form. You will learn how state changes update the screen and how to move between screens.
learn: `StatefulWidget` and `setState` for data that changes
Navigating between screens with `Navigator.push` and returning results with `Navigator.pop`
Forms with `TextFormField`, a category dropdown, a date picker and validation
Swipe-to-delete with `Dismissible` and undo with `SnackBar`
steps: Make the dashboard a `StatefulWidget` that owns the transaction list.
Add a `FloatingActionButton` that opens an `AddTransactionScreen` with fields for title, amount, category dropdown, an income/expense toggle, and a date picker using `showDatePicker`.
Validate the form: title required, amount must be a number greater than zero.
Return the new transaction with `Navigator.pop(context, transaction)` and add it inside `setState`; check that the balance card updates.
Reuse the same form for editing: tap a transaction to open the form pre-filled, and replace the old item on save.
Add swipe-to-delete with `Dismissible` and a `SnackBar` with an Undo action.
Record a short screen recording of adding, editing and deleting a transaction.
deliverables: An Add/Edit Transaction form with validation and a date picker
Edit by tapping a transaction and delete by swiping
A balance card that updates after every change
A 30-60 second screen recording
done_when: Invalid input (empty title, zero or text amount) shows an error and is not saved
A new transaction appears in the list and the balance changes immediately
Editing a transaction updates it in place instead of creating a duplicate
Swiping deletes a transaction and Undo restores it
hints: If the screen does not refresh, make sure the list change happens inside `setState`.
Pass an optional existing `Transaction` into the form screen; if it is not null, you are editing.
Use `double.tryParse` for the amount so bad input returns null instead of throwing.
Search 'Flutter cookbook forms' in the [Flutter docs](https://docs.flutter.dev) for a validation example.
2.stretch: Add a search bar that filters transactions by title as you type.
post_highlights: Added a validated add and edit transaction form to my Flutter finance app
Implemented swipe-to-delete with undo using Dismissible and SnackBar
Used StatefulWidget and navigation results to keep the balance updated in real time

3.title: Local Database & Monthly View
3.goal: Save transactions on the device so they survive restarts, and add a month selector so users can see one month at a time. You will also handle loading and error cases so the app always shows something sensible.
learn: Storing data on the device with Hive or `sqflite`
Async Dart with `Future`, `async` and `await`
Converting model objects to and from maps or JSON
Filtering data by date and showing loading, empty and error states
steps: Choose Hive (works on Android and Chrome) or `sqflite` (Android/iOS only, uses SQL); pick Hive if you run on Chrome.
Add `toMap()`/`fromMap()` (or a Hive adapter) and give each transaction a unique `id` so edits and deletes target the right record.
Create a `TransactionRepository` class with `getAll`, `add`, `update` and `delete` methods, and test it with a few `print` calls.
Load transactions at startup with a loading spinner, then save through the repository on every add, edit and delete.
Fully restart the app to confirm data is kept.
Add a month selector (previous/next arrows) and show only that month's transactions and totals.
Use `try/catch` around database calls and show a friendly error message or `SnackBar` on failure, plus an empty-state message for months with no transactions.
deliverables: Transactions stored in a local database
A `TransactionRepository` class for all data access
A month selector that filters the list and totals
Loading, empty and error states
done_when: Transactions are still there after fully closing and reopening the app
Editing and deleting change the correct saved record
Switching months shows only that month's transactions and correct totals
A month with no data shows an empty-state message
Database errors are caught and shown without crashing
hints: Hot reload does not prove persistence; always stop and restart the app to test.
Generate ids with `DateTime.now().millisecondsSinceEpoch.toString()` if you do not want another package.
Compare `date.year` and `date.month` to filter a month instead of comparing full dates.
Read the example tab of each package on [pub.dev](https://pub.dev) before writing your own code.
3.stretch: Add a Settings screen where the user can clear all data after a confirmation dialog.
post_highlights: Added a local database to my Flutter finance app so data persists across restarts
Built a repository layer and a month-by-month transaction view
Handled loading, empty and error states for reliable user experience

4.title: Budgets, Pie Chart & Release Build
4.goal: Turn WalletWave into a finished portfolio app. You will move data into a Provider, add a category pie chart and a monthly budget warning, polish the design, and ship an installable build with a demo.
learn: App-wide state management with `provider` and `ChangeNotifier`
Grouping data by category and drawing a pie chart with a package such as `fl_chart`
Comparing spending against a saved budget limit
Building a release APK or web build
steps: Create a `TransactionProvider extends ChangeNotifier` that uses your repository and calls `notifyListeners()` after changes.
Wrap the app in `ChangeNotifierProvider` and read data with `context.watch`/`context.read` instead of passing lists around; retest all old features.
Add an Insights screen that groups the selected month's expenses by category and shows a pie chart with a legend.
Let the user set a monthly budget (save it with `shared_preferences`), show a progress bar of spent vs budget, and turn it red with a warning when over 80%.
Polish: consistent colours, an app icon and name, and a dark theme.
Build with `flutter build apk --release` (or `flutter build web` without the Android SDK) and test the build.
Write a README with features, screenshots and setup, and record a 60-second demo.
deliverables: State managed with Provider
An Insights screen with a category pie chart
A monthly budget with progress bar and warning
A release APK or web build, README and 60-second demo video
done_when: Transaction data flows through a Provider rather than constructors
The pie chart slices match the category totals for the selected month
The budget bar updates after adding an expense and shows a warning past 80%
The budget value is still set after restarting the app
A release build is available from the repo with a complete README
hints: Build a `Map<String, double>` of category totals first and print it before drawing the chart.
Skip categories with zero spending, or the pie chart may look empty or error out.
Attach the APK to a GitHub Release so anyone can download it.
The deployment section of the [Flutter docs](https://docs.flutter.dev) covers Android and web release builds.
4.stretch: Add an Export button that creates a CSV of the month's transactions and opens the share sheet.
post_highlights: Completed WalletWave, a Flutter expense tracker with local storage and Provider
Built a category spending pie chart and a monthly budget warning
Shipped a release build with a documented README and demo video

tracks.project_name: RecipeRadar: Recipe Finder App with a Free Public API
tracks.tagline: Build a recipe app that searches real recipes from a free online API and lets you save your favourites.

1.title: Recipe Screens with Sample Data
1.goal: Set up Flutter and build the two main screens of RecipeRadar, a recipe grid and a recipe detail page, using a few hardcoded recipes. You will learn layouts and images so the app looks good before any internet code is added.
learn: How a Flutter app is structured: `MaterialApp`, `Scaffold` and the widget tree
Layouts with `Column`, `Row`, `Stack`, `Padding` and `Expanded`
Showing grids and images with `GridView.builder` and `Image.network`
Creating a Dart model class and a reusable widget
steps: Install Flutter, run `flutter doctor`, create the project with `flutter create reciperadar`, and run the default app once.
Choose where to run it: Android emulator, a real phone over USB, or Chrome with `flutter run -d chrome` on low-spec laptops.
Create a `Recipe` class with `id`, `name`, `category`, `area`, `imageUrl`, `ingredients` and `instructions`, and hardcode 4-6 recipes with real image URLs.
Build a `HomeScreen` with a `GridView.builder` of recipe cards showing the image and name.
Move the card into its own `RecipeCard` widget file with rounded corners and a fixed image height.
Build a `RecipeDetailScreen` layout with a large image, name, category tags, an ingredients list and the instructions in a scrollable page.
Push to a public GitHub repo with a README and screenshots.
deliverables: A Flutter project in a public GitHub repo
A home screen showing a grid of recipe cards
A recipe detail screen layout
A README with screenshots
done_when: The app runs without errors on an emulator, phone or Chrome
The grid is built from a Dart list using `GridView.builder`
Recipe images load and keep a consistent size
The detail screen scrolls without overflow errors on a small phone size
The README includes screenshots
hints: Use `ClipRRect` for rounded image corners and `BoxFit.cover` so images fill their space neatly.
Wrap long pages in `SingleChildScrollView` to avoid the yellow-black overflow stripe.
The [Flutter docs](https://docs.flutter.dev) widget catalog shows every layout widget with examples.
1.stretch: Make the grid show 2 columns on phones and 4 columns on wide screens using `MediaQuery` or `LayoutBuilder`.
post_highlights: Built the UI of a Flutter recipe app with a responsive recipe grid
Designed a scrollable recipe detail page with images and ingredient lists
Created a reusable recipe card widget and Dart data model

2.title: Navigation, Search & Favourites
2.goal: Connect the screens and make the app interactive: tapping a card opens its details, a search box filters recipes, and users can mark favourites. This week is about state and navigation, still with sample data.
learn: `StatefulWidget` and `setState` for changing data
Navigating with `Navigator.push` and passing a recipe to the next screen
Handling text input with `TextField` and `onChanged`
Using a bottom navigation bar to switch between tabs
steps: Open `RecipeDetailScreen` with `Navigator.push` when a card is tapped, passing the selected `Recipe` through the constructor.
Add a search `TextField` at the top of the home screen that filters the grid by name as the user types, using `setState`.
Show a friendly 'No recipes found' message when the filter returns nothing.
Add a heart `IconButton` on the detail screen and cards that toggles a recipe in a favourites list.
Add a `BottomNavigationBar` with Home and Favourites tabs, and show only favourite recipes on the Favourites tab.
Keep the favourites list in the parent widget that holds the bottom navigation so both tabs see the same data.
Record a short video of searching, opening a recipe and adding a favourite.
deliverables: Working navigation from grid to detail and back
Live search filtering with an empty-state message
A Favourites tab showing favourited recipes
A 30-60 second screen recording
done_when: Tapping any card opens the correct recipe's details
Typing in the search box filters the grid immediately and clearing it shows all recipes
A search with no matches shows an empty-state message
Favouriting a recipe makes it appear on the Favourites tab and unfavouriting removes it
hints: Filter with `where` and `toLowerCase()` on both the recipe name and the query for case-insensitive search.
If the Favourites tab does not update, the favourites list is probably stored in a child widget instead of the shared parent.
Search 'Flutter cookbook navigation' in the [Flutter docs](https://docs.flutter.dev) for passing data between screens.
2.stretch: Add category filter chips (for example Vegetarian, Dessert, Chicken) above the grid.
post_highlights: Added navigation and live search to my Flutter recipe app
Built a favourites feature with a separate tab using StatefulWidget
Handled empty search results with a clear empty-state message

3.title: Real Recipes from a Public API
3.goal: Replace the sample data with real recipes from TheMealDB, a free recipe API that needs no sign-up for testing. You will make HTTP requests, parse JSON, and handle loading and error states the way real apps do.
learn: Making HTTP GET requests with the `http` package
Parsing JSON into Dart objects with a `fromJson` factory
Async Dart and `FutureBuilder` for loading data
Handling loading, empty, error and no-internet states
steps: Open TheMealDB search URL for a word like 'chicken' (`https://www.themealdb.com/api/json/v1/1/search.php?s=chicken`) in your browser and study the JSON before writing any code.
Add the `http` package and write a `RecipeApi` class with a `searchRecipes(String query)` method that returns `Future<List<Recipe>>`.
Write `Recipe.fromJson` to map fields like `idMeal`, `strMeal`, `strMealThumb`, `strCategory` and `strInstructions`, and loop over `strIngredient1`..`strIngredient20` to build the ingredients list.
Print the parsed list in the console first, then show it in the grid using `FutureBuilder` with a loading spinner.
Connect the search box to the API so pressing search (not every keystroke) fetches new results.
Handle errors: check the status code, catch exceptions, and show an error message with a Retry button; note that the API returns `null` for meals when nothing matches.
Remove the hardcoded sample recipes once the API works.
deliverables: A `RecipeApi` class that fetches and parses real recipes
Search that returns live results from the API
Loading, empty and error states with a Retry button
Updated README explaining the API used
done_when: The home screen shows real recipes from the API on launch
Searching a dish name returns matching recipes from the API
A search with no results shows an empty-state message instead of crashing
Turning off the internet and searching shows an error message with Retry
The detail screen shows ingredients and instructions from the API data
hints: The API returns `{"meals": null}` when nothing is found, so check for null before looping.
Trigger the search from `onSubmitted` or a search button to avoid sending a request on every keystroke.
If Chrome shows a network or CORS error, test on an Android emulator or phone to confirm your code is correct.
The `http` package page on [pub.dev](https://pub.dev) has a short GET example.
3.stretch: Add a 'Random recipe' button that calls the API's random endpoint and opens the result.
post_highlights: Connected my Flutter recipe app to a public REST API
Parsed JSON into Dart models and displayed live results with FutureBuilder
Handled loading, empty and offline error states with a retry option

4.title: Provider, Saved Favourites & Release
4.goal: Finish RecipeRadar as a portfolio-ready app. Favourites will move into a Provider and be saved on the device, then you will polish the app and ship an installable build with a demo video.
learn: App-wide state management with `provider` and `ChangeNotifier`
Saving favourites locally with `shared_preferences`
Small polish touches such as a dark theme and image placeholders
Building a release APK or web build
steps: Create a `FavouritesProvider extends ChangeNotifier` with `toggle`, `isFavourite` and a list of favourite recipes, and wrap the app in `ChangeNotifierProvider`.
Replace the favourites list you passed through constructors with `context.watch`/`context.read`, and retest the heart buttons on both tabs.
Save favourites with `shared_preferences` as a JSON list (store id, name and image), load them at startup, and confirm they survive a restart.
Make the Favourites tab work offline by showing the saved data instead of calling the API.
Polish: image loading placeholders, an error icon for broken images, a dark theme, and an app icon and name.
Build with `flutter build apk --release` (or `flutter build web`) and test it.
Write a README with features, screenshots, the API credit and setup steps, and record a 60-second demo.
deliverables: Favourites managed with Provider
Favourites saved on the device and available offline
A release APK or web build
A polished README and 60-second demo video
done_when: Favourites are managed through a Provider
Favourites are still there after fully restarting the app
The Favourites tab shows saved recipes with the internet turned off
Broken images show a placeholder instead of an error
A release build and complete README are available in the repo
hints: Save only the fields you need for the favourites list; you can fetch full details again when online.
Use `errorBuilder` on `Image.network` to handle broken image links.
Attach the APK to a GitHub Release so recruiters can install it.
See the deployment section of the [Flutter docs](https://docs.flutter.dev) for release builds.
4.stretch: Add a shopping list screen where users can tick off ingredients from a recipe, saved locally.
post_highlights: Completed RecipeRadar, a Flutter recipe finder powered by a public API
Managed favourites with Provider and saved them on the device for offline use
Shipped a release build with a documented README and demo video
